candidate: 512-thread decode attention block (16 key classes instead of 8), keys-per-tile 2, with the denominator reduction pinned to the block kernel's 256 lanes
reason: pass 1's shuffle tree was the measured bottleneck (108 us of the 318 us sliding launch, with all loads and FMAs still live) and it is latency-bound, not throughput-bound, because 8 warps per block cannot hide it. Doubling the warps per block gives sliding 318.9 -> 288.4 us and full 339.8 -> 270.1 us at keys=1024, full 509.5 -> 399 us at keys=2048. Campaign metric 41.9049 -> 43.6297 tok/s (+4.1%), +171% over the 16.0931 baseline

mechanism.diagnosis: clean ablations of the iteration-23 kernel, each keeping the data dependencies alive so the compiler cannot delete the measured work: replacing the shuffle tree with in-lane adds (all loads and FMAs still live) saved 108 us of 318 at sliding and 75 us of 354 at full; removing pass 1's LDS logit store saved nothing; skipping the pass-2 loop entirely saved nothing; replacing the K loads with a constant saved only 25-31 us. So the tree was the single largest item and the K loads were already fine
mechanism.cause: the tree issues 40 warp-wide shuffles per key (8 elements x 5 shuffle levels) and is a dependent chain per key, so it needs many warps in flight to hide its latency. The block had 8 warps and the launch has one block per (token, head) - 16 blocks for a decode step - leaving the machine mostly idle
mechanism.fix: kThreads 256 -> 512, so the block has 16 key classes and each warp walks half as many keys while still evaluating the full 256-lane tree per key. Only the key-class split changed: every key's own reduction order is untouched, so the kernel stays bit-exact
mechanism.second_fix: keys-per-tile re-swept at the new block size: 2/4/8 -> 290.3/294.1/303.1 us sliding and 271.2/280.4/422.2 us full, so 2 replaces 4
mechanism.denominator_pinning: gemma4_decode_tree1's addition order depends on its lane count, so a 512-thread block would have rounded the denominator differently from the block kernel and stopped being bit-exact (measured: 3.3% of elements off by 1-2 bf16 ulps). Pass 2 now runs its 256-lane partition and tree with the block kernel's lane count on group 0 only, while the other 256-thread groups execute gemma4_decode_tree1 with an empty sum purely so that all threads reach its barriers; every thread reads group 0's result from `partial[0]`. The LDS layout reserves one 256-float denominator region per group
rejected: level-major interleaving of the four in-flight trees (bit-exact, since the keys are independent): no gain at sliding and 11% worse at full, so the compiler was already interleaving and the extra live registers cost more than they bought
1024-thread blocks: 298.6 us sliding and 289.2 us full, worse than 512 on both

16-byte vector loads for pass 1's K octet (one load instead of eight per key per half): neutral at 325.1 us sliding and 340.6 us full against 318.9 and 339.8, consistent with the K loads costing only 25-31 us

correctness.contract: bit-exact with the block kernel (same-schedule arithmetic): only the key-class split, the keys-per-tile, and which threads compute the (now pinned) denominator changed
correctness.parity_result: green together with tests/test_gpu_gemma4_attention_geometry.py - bitwise equality on every shape, both dtypes, keep and holes masks, keys 1..8192
correctness.note: the first two 512-thread attempts failed parity (100% of elements, then 3.3% off by 1-2 bf16 ulps) and both causes are recorded above: an undersized denominator region that overran max_s, and the unpinned reduction order. Parity was the gate that caught them; the campaign row numbers were never taken from a non-parity state
correctness.public_path_parity: true on all four re-measured campaign rows
